entries.note: “Dumbest money” is a judgment of worth; the desperation inference is also explicitly probabilistic.
This bundles financial assertions with a subjective verdict about meaningful products. The profit-history assertion could be checked separately.

entries.test: Published revenue and expense figures would establish whether the stated current cost-to-revenue ratio implies over $27 billion in costs for $11.6 billion in revenue.
entries.note: This is a conditional calculation, not an unconditional prediction of actual 2025 spending.
Both the cost increase and accompanying free-user growth are explicitly qualified as likely.

entries.test: Financial reporting following the specified subscription price increases would show whether the added revenue materially reduces OpenAI's losses.
entries.note: The claim depends on the specified hikes and gives no deadline.

entries.test: Disclosed or credibly reported training costs for subsequent, more complex models would show whether they reach hundreds of millions of dollars or a billion dollars.
entries.note: This is a firm cost forecast without a deadline.
“Truly important” and “particularly impressive” express subjective evaluations.
The cost prediction is independently testable, but this combined proposition also requires judging whether a use case is meaningful.

entries.test: Public training-data disclosures, data-supply studies and comparative model evaluations would establish whether substantially shared, diminishing training data is making model outputs increasingly similar.
entries.note: The asserted relationship is empirical, even if establishing it is difficult.

entries.test: OpenAI's revenue and user-growth series through October 2024, alongside historical company growth records, would test the asserted growth slowdown and absence of comparable sustained growth.
entries.note: Read in context, this advances an assessment of public growth evidence rather than merely reporting a private belief.

entries.test: Public cost and usage data across increasing deployment sizes would show whether generative AI serving costs per comparable user decline as customer counts rise.
entries.note: He attributes the claimed absence of economies of scale to per-user computing requirements.
Expressing concern does not specify a business outcome that would settle it.
The claim evaluates whether the revenue is bad or exciting.
“Table stakes” evaluates how impressive the subscriber count should be given brand prominence.
Whether differences are dramatic or use cases compelling depends on evaluative standards.
“Terrible at product” is an evaluative verdict.
He offers a likely classification and a general claim about household spending, rather than a specific future event.
“Not a great business” supplies no agreed standard of business quality.
The combined claim depends on subjective judgments about endearment and a killer app. Its competitor assertion could be examined separately.

entries.test: Reported ChatGPT paid-user counts and subscription prices through the end of 2025 would show whether OpenAI achieved the described expansion of roughly 18 million additional paying users at $22 per month.
entries.note: “I do not think this company is capable” expresses a substantive negative forecast, not an explicit probability estimate. The surrounding revenue discussion supplies the 2025 horizon.

entries.test: Contemporaneous API revenue, paying-customer counts and integration usage data would show whether OpenAI faced low integration demand or low revenue from connected companies.
entries.note: “Suggests” introduces an evidence-based inference; the drafter's “likely” label is not the author's wording.

entries.test: Comparable monthly API revenue figures for OpenAI and Azure OpenAI through October 2024 would establish whether OpenAI's growth plateaued and their model-access revenues were approximately equal.
entries.note: This is an empirical inference about revenue levels and trends.
The normalization incorporates the following sentence's explicitly tentative alternative, “Or, perhaps,” about customer preferences.
“There may not even be” states a possibility, while market share is also presented as a wager.
The disjunction includes judgments of usefulness, attractiveness and impressiveness without a shared standard.

entries.test: Segment revenue, serving expenses, margins and retention data would establish whether OpenAI's API business was substantially less financially viable than its ChatGPT subscription business.
entries.note: Acknowledging uncertainty does not by itself turn an asserted financial comparison into a probability claim.

entries.test: OpenAI's reported 2024 server costs and revenue would show whether server costs alone consumed at least all revenue.
entries.note: The statement is Zitron's inference from reported estimates.

entries.test: Public financing announcements and financial reporting through July 2025 would show whether, after the current round, OpenAI needed and raised another round at least as large.
entries.note: “I believe” introduces a firm “will have to” forecast; the drafter's “likely” modality understates it.
The main conclusion explicitly assigns an extremely low likelihood to a quick fix.
The proposed raise size is explicitly “likely,” so the combined numerical prediction is not firm throughout.

entries.test: OpenAI's expansion activity and financing announcements through mid-2025 would show whether continued growth required another round larger than its October 2024 round at a higher valuation.
entries.note: The deadline, larger round and higher valuation are firm commitments. The illustrative dollar amounts remain explicitly probabilistic.

entries.test: An OpenAI public listing, or public evidence of durable investor returns through a route other than listing or secondary sales, would test the asserted need to go public.
entries.note: “At some point” supplies no deadline; the secondary-sale exception must be preserved.

entries.test: Financing disclosures after the described restructuring, subsequent raise and public listing would show whether OpenAI still required additional funding rounds.
entries.note: This is an undated forecast tied to completion of the preceding steps.

entries.test: Contemporaneous product comparisons, switching costs, customer retention and competing model availability would establish whether ChatGPT Plus lacked durable competitive barriers and meaningful differentiation beyond voice.
entries.note: “Moat” has an ordinary business reading as a durable competitive advantage.

entries.test: Contemporaneous API prices, competitor capabilities and customer demand responses would show whether OpenAI lacked pricing power because comparable substitutes were available.
entries.note: The plain reading concerns commercial pricing power, not the technical ability to edit a price list.
This is an emphatic characterization of the company and its staff, with no distinct testable commitment.

entries.test: Contemporaneous developer adoption, integration usage, paying-user counts and spending would show whether meaningful developer and user interest existed despite the cited revenue level.
entries.note: “Heavily suggests” presents an inference about observable demand, not an explicit chance estimate.
The sentence asserts the failure as the premise of asking why it happened. “Really cool” is a subjective standard.

entries.test: ChatGPT Plus paid-user and revenue figures through 2025 would show whether it achieved the growth rate identified in the post as necessary for OpenAI's revenue target.
entries.note: The surrounding calculations give the otherwise implicit growth rate and horizon. This is a negative feasibility forecast rather than an explicit probability statement.
The combined prediction explicitly concerns reduced likelihood of integration and a likely decline in ChatGPT interest.
The overall verdict mixes evaluative language with an independently testable assertion about losses per interaction.

entries.test: OpenAI's operating status on October 2, 2026, together with documented material changes to its economics or energy and compute efficiency, would test the conditional two-year survival forecast.
entries.note: The deadline has passed. The exception covers significant changes generally, not only the two examples given.
“Might” qualifies a possible present lack of a viable business; no future outcome is explicitly specified.

entries.test: Public evidence available by October 2024 about sustained paid subscriptions, renewals and retention would show whether there was evidence supporting long-term payment by millions of users.
entries.note: This challenges the available evidence; it does not firmly predict that millions will never pay long-term.
